title: From les Parcours to Parkour: Lisses, the Wall, and the Discipline That Left Home
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Hue, a son born to the colonial army
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikidata Q7298587 gives Raymond Belle born 30 October 1939 at Hue and dead December 1999 at Villeneuve-Saint-Georges. English Wikipedia's 'Raymond Belle' is a redirect to Parkour#History, not an article, and supplies only the bare year and country. This stop belongs to Raymond, not to David: it stands at the head of the file as the inheritance David is born into, not as a place David went.
stops.campa: In the imperial city on the Perfume River, in a French Indochina with fifteen years left to run, Raymond Belle is born on the thirtieth of October. His father is a French soldier. His mother is Vietnamese. What the boy carries out of this country in the end is not a memory of it but a method, learned the hard way and never afterward explained: a body has to be able to get itself out of anywhere. He passes that on, thirty-four years later, to a son born in Normandy who never sees the place. The war that will take both parents from him has not started yet.
suggested_refs: Wikidata Q7298587, 'Raymond Belle', French soldier and firefighter (1939-1999)
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Parkour', section History (Raymond Belle redirect target)

stops.name: Da Lat, the military orphanage
stops.date_confidence: attested as fact, approximate as date. English Wikipedia's parkour history gives the sequence (father killed, separation from the mother, placement in a French military orphanage at Da Lat at around seven) without a year; 1946 is derived from the 1939 birth and 'around age seven' and should be read as c. 1946-47. Month and day are placeholders. Raymond's stop, not David's.
stops.campa: His father is killed and his mother lost to him in the First Indochina War, and the army that made the family takes charge of what is left of it. At about seven Raymond Belle is placed in a French military orphanage in the hill station of Da Lat, where the children of soldiers are drilled like soldiers. He learns to climb, to run, to fall, to carry, because the school is built to teach it and because a boy with no family and no country is better off strong. In 1954, after the fall of Dien Bien Phu, he is put on a ship for France.
suggested_refs: The French military orphanage system in Indochina, and the 1954 evacuations after Dien Bien Phu

stops.name: Paris, the fire brigade and les parcours
stops.date_confidence: inferred date, attested fact. The sources say only that Raymond Belle remained in military education until nineteen, when he joined the Brigade de sapeurs-pompiers de Paris. With a 30 October 1939 birth, nineteen spans October 1958 to October 1959; no source reached gives a year, so this pin is dated to his nineteenth birthday purely to order the segment. The Paris coordinate is the canonical placeholder pin used across the atlas, not the caserne, which is not identified in any source reached. Hebert's influence on French military and firefighter physical culture is stated by English Wikipedia; no personal contact between Hebert and Raymond Belle is evidenced anywhere.
stops.campa: At nineteen he joins the Brigade de sapeurs-pompiers de Paris, a unit of the French Army. Raymond Belle takes the drill further than the drill requires: alone, at night, off the roster, he runs what he calls les parcours, courses of his own devising through the training ground and the city. Nobody names the practice, because it is not yet a practice; it is one fireman keeping himself alive. The doctrine of the house he trains inside was set two generations earlier by Georges Hebert. Walk, run, jump, climb, balance, throw, lift, swim, defend, and be strong to be useful.
suggested_refs: Georges Hebert's methode naturelle as adopted into French military and fire-brigade training
The Brigade de sapeurs-pompiers de Paris, an army unit
sources: georges_hebert.journey.json, stop 'Lorient, the fusiliers marins and the ten families of movement' (1904)

stops.name: Notre-Dame de Paris, the flag on the tower
stops.date_confidence: tradition, not confirmed. Repeated across parkour community histories and family lore; no source reachable in this research confirms it, and a French Wikipedia fetch for Raymond Belle returned 404. The year 1969 comes from that tradition alone; month and day are placeholders. The coordinate is the atlas's existing Notre-Dame pin. Raymond's episode, told to David; not a place David went.
stops.campa: Tradition in the fire brigade, and in every history parkour has since written of itself, holds that a Viet Cong flag is hung on a tower of Notre-Dame de Paris and that Raymond Belle is lowered on a helicopter cable to take it down, and is decorated for it. No document reached in this research confirms any part of it. The story is told anyway, in Lisses and in the barracks, to a boy who will not properly meet his father for years, and it is the shape of the father he gets: a man who goes up the outside of the cathedral. Who first told it, and whether Raymond told it himself, no source reached can say.
suggested_refs: The Notre-Dame flag episode as repeated in parkour community histories, unconfirmed in any primary source located
sources: Parkour community tradition, not independently confirmed

stops.name: Fecamp, born in the port
stops.date_confidence: attested. Birth date and place given by English and French Wikipedia alike. Note that davidbelleparkour.com, refetched directly, gives the date only and states no birthplace, so it cannot corroborate Fecamp. Two coordinates for the same town circulate in this dossier, 49.7593 / 0.3735 and 49.7599 / 0.3757, about 500 m apart; the first is used here and the discrepancy is recorded rather than hidden.
stops.campa: David Nicolas Belle is born on the twenty-ninth of April in the Normandy fishing port of Fecamp, under the chalk cliffs, to Monique Kitten and Raymond Belle. The mother's line is French and English. Her father Gilbert Kitten is a sergeant-major of the Paris fire brigade, so there are firemen on both sides of the child. His parents do not stay together. He grows up largely away from Raymond, hearing about him rather than being raised by him, which is a different education and a harder one to get out from under. Nothing in Fecamp marks any of this; no source consulted records a plaque in the town.
suggested_refs: Fecamp, Seine-Maritime; no plaque or monument to Belle was found there in any source consulted

stops.name: Les Sables-d'Olonne, the contested first years
stops.date_confidence: unverified, and in direct conflict with the Fecamp-Normandy account. Found only in a secondary promotional biography; not corroborated by English Wikipedia or by the official site's own about page, both fetched directly. The date is an arbitrary marker inside the claimed period c. 1973-1987 and carries no evidential weight. Included rather than dropped because the conflict is genuine and unresolved.
stops.campa: Some accounts of his childhood put the first fourteen years not in Normandy at all but on the Atlantic at Les Sables-d'Olonne, another port, another seafront, the same weather. The two chronologies cannot both be true and no source reached settles them. What they agree on is the shape: a coastal childhood at a distance from Paris, from the fire brigade and from the father, and a boy who arrives in the Essonne suburbs from somewhere with cliffs in it. Which coast it was is still open, and nothing reached can choose between the two chronologies.
suggested_refs: The unresolved conflict between the Fecamp and Les Sables-d'Olonne childhood chronologies
sources: Secondary promotional biography, uncorroborated; contradicted by English Wikipedia, 'David Belle'

stops.name: Lisses, the planned town
stops.date_confidence: attested arrival, contested age. English Wikipedia gives age eleven, hence 1984; other secondary biographies give fourteen or fifteen. The contradiction is live and is not resolved here. Month and day are placeholders. Coordinates are the corrected figures for Lisses (48.5981 N, 2.4244 E per English Wikipedia and Nominatim), replacing the 48.5844 / 2.3985 that circulated in the dossier, which is about 2.3 km off.
stops.campa: Lisses is a planned town in the Essonne, run up quickly south of Paris in concrete and grass: low blocks, ramps, service stairs, retaining walls, handrails, and gaps between roofs of exactly the wrong width. Its planners assumed that people would walk around things. David Belle arrives as a boy, at eleven by one account and at fourteen or fifteen by others, and starts reading the town the other way, as a surface with a grain to it. He is still living in Lisses forty years later.
suggested_refs: English Wikipedia, 'Lisses': 'Parkour was developed in Lisses and nearby Courcouronnes, having been created by David Belle, who has resided in Lisses since the 1980s.'

stops.name: Courcouronnes, the Dame du Lac
stops.date_confidence: site attested, date approximate, anecdote unverified. The Dame du Lac is Pierre Szekely's climbing sculpture in the lake park at Evry-Courcouronnes, not in Lisses as much of the parkour literature repeats; coordinates from OSM, 48.6132 / 2.4219. The date is a marker inside the late 1980s and early 1990s training years. The exchange with Raymond traces to Alec Wilkinson's 2007 New Yorker profile, which could not be fetched in this research; treat it as family tradition.
stops.campa: In the lake park at Courcouronnes stands a climbing sculpture by Pierre Szekely, concrete slabs and holes and ledges, called the Dame du Lac, built to be climbed and later closed to the public. Belle trains on it for years. The rule he says he works to is four clauses long and it is a fireman's rule rather than an athlete's. Family tradition holds that he shows his father a move on this stone and is told that Raymond was doing the same thing at nine.
stops.quote: Faire, faire bien, faire vite et bien
stops.quote_source: David Belle, davidbelleparkour.com, About page, under the English heading 'Do it, Do it well, Do it Fast and Well'
suggested_refs: Pierre Szekely's Dame du Lac, parc du lac, Evry-Courcouronnes, now closed to the public
Wikiquote's variant, cited to americanparkour.com: 'First, do it. Second, do it well. Third, do it well and fast'

stops.name: Evry, the courtyards and the stairwells
stops.date_confidence: attested in general, unattested in detail. That the training extended from Lisses into Evry is stated by the official site and by parkour.com; no source consulted names an individual building, courtyard or stairwell. The date is a marker inside the late 1980s and 1990s.
stops.campa: The training spreads out of Lisses into neighbouring Evry: courtyards, garage roofs, stairwells, the backs of buildings where nobody is watching. No source names the individual walls, which is fitting, since the entire proposition is that any wall will do. Boys turn up at the same places at the same hours and compete in a currency with no exchange rate outside the group, which is the ability to cross something the person beside you cannot cross. There is no club, no coach, no membership and no fee.
suggested_refs: The housing estates of Evry and Lisses as the first training ground of the discipline
sources: parkour.com, 'The Definitive Origin of Parkour: David Belle's Legacy'

segments.name: The Uniforms That Did Not Hold

stops.name: Lisses, leaving school at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: reported, largely self-sourced. French Wikipedia gives the departure from school at about fifteen, the move toward Paris, national service, a first-aid certificate and a UFOLEP gymnastics diploma. The underlying certificates were not located. The date is derived from the 1973 birth and 'about fifteen'; month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He leaves school at about fifteen. The record of what follows is thin and mostly self-reported: a first-aid certificate, a UFOLEP gymnastics diploma, a drift toward Paris and toward the institutions his family has always joined. He is not a boy in flight from discipline. He is a boy trying to enter the exact discipline his grandfather, his father and his half-brother entered, by the door they used, and he will fail to get through it twice before he builds one of his own. Neither certificate has been located in any archive reached.
suggested_refs: The UFOLEP gymnastics diploma and first-aid certificate, reported but not located

stops.name: Paris, the fire brigade and the injury
stops.date_confidence: attested, undated. French Wikipedia states that Belle followed his grandfather Gilbert Kitten, his father and his brother Jean-Francois into the Paris Fire Brigade and was suspended after an injury without resuming; it does not name the injury, does not report the 'too many rules' remark, and gives no year, but places the episode before the Vannes service. The 1989 date orders the segment and nothing more. The Paris coordinate is the canonical placeholder pin; no caserne is identified in any source reached.
stops.campa: He follows his grandfather Gilbert Kitten, his father Raymond and his half-brother Jean-Francois into the Brigade de sapeurs-pompiers de Paris. He is injured during the training, suspended, and does not resume. Three generations of the family have gone up ladders for the city of Paris and he is not going to be the fourth. Everything he does afterward is the fire brigade's method carried out with no fire, no crew, no orders and no wage, on the walls of a suburb, for reasons he will spend the rest of his life being asked to explain.
suggested_refs: The Belle and Kitten family service in the Brigade de sapeurs-pompiers de Paris across three generations

stops.name: Vannes, the marine infantry and the rope
stops.date_confidence: service attested, details and dates not. Both English and French Wikipedia confirm service in a Troupes de marine regiment at Vannes, including honours for rope climbing and the obstacle course; no source reached gives a year, and the 'c. 1989-1991' range that circulates in the dossier is unsourced. The regimental rope record said to have been held by Raymond, the gymnastics certificate and an Essonne obstacle-course championship are self-reported and were not found in any military record. The 'too many rules' remark is not in either Wikipedia.
stops.campa: He enlists in a marine infantry regiment garrisoned at Vannes in Brittany. What he brings home is a set of stories his own sources tell and no archive confirms: a regimental rope-climbing record previously held by Raymond, honours on the obstacle course, a certificate for gymnastic ability. The parcours du combattant, the army's assault course, is the object he grew up beside without knowing it, and the word for the thing he does will be cut down out of its name. He leaves the regiment. Too many rules, he says.
suggested_refs: The parcours du combattant, the French army assault course, from which the word parkour is taken

stops.name: India, three months in the trees
stops.date_confidence: undated, unlocated, and internally contradictory. English Wikipedia says only three months in India studying kung fu; French Wikipedia places it after national service and repeats the black belt. No source reached gives a year or a city, and the research pool dates the same trip to c. 1991-1992 in one lens and c. 1996-1997 in another, a contradiction left open. The coordinate is a country centroid used as an honest placeholder because no place is actually known; it is not a claim about where he was. The 1992 date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: At some point after the army he goes to India, for three months by one account and six by another. He trains in trees. He watches monkeys climb and, more to the point, watches how they land. He is said to have come home with a black belt in kung fu, which no document supports. The episode has since become a fixed station of parkour's founding story, retold with complete confidence by writers who have never had a place to attach it to. No source reached names the city, the region or the year.
suggested_refs: The India episode as an undated and unlocated element of parkour's founding narrative

segments.name: The Circle, the Name, and the Division

stops.name: Lisses, the circle of cousins
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. English Wikipedia's parkour article places the formation of the group loosely in this period and names Chau Belle-Dinh and Williams Belle among the cousins; no source reached gives a founding date, and the group's own accounts differ on who was present when. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Back in Lisses he gathers what there is: cousins, half-brothers, neighbours, boys from Evry. Chau Belle-Dinh, Williams Belle, Sebastien Foucan and others train with him in the estates most evenings. The test is not style; it is whether the movement would still work with something behind you, at night, in the wet, carrying somebody. Nothing is written down. The discipline is transmitted the way a trade is transmitted, by watching an older boy do a thing and then doing it until it is yours.
stops.quote: At the physical end, Parkour is getting over all the obstacles in your path as you would in an emergency situation.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to David Belle, cited to parkour.net via Wikiquote; the parkour.net URL no longer resolves and the wording could not be checked against the original
suggested_refs: The founding Lisses and Evry training circle, later known as Yamakasi

stops.name: Evry, the traverse in eight hours
stops.date_confidence: community tradition, promotional source, untimed. The eight-hour Lisses to Evry traverse appears in parkour.com's 'The Definitive Origin of Parkour: David Belle's Legacy', a Belle-partisan site, and is not independently corroborated; no source gives a date. The date orders the segment. The quote is attributed to Belle via Wikiquote, citing a parkour.net page that no longer resolves.
stops.campa: A story told about these years by the parkour community, and by Belle's own partisans, has him crossing the whole distance from Lisses to Evry over the built landscape rather than through it, roofs and rails and walls, in eight hours. Nobody outside the circle timed it, and no source gives a date. The claim matters less than the standard it fixes, which is a return standard and not a stunt standard: the crossing counts only if the man who made it could have made it back. A jump you survive once is not a jump. It is an accident you got away with.
stops.quote: If you go from A to B, you need to be able to get back from B to A.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to David Belle, cited to parkour.net via Wikiquote; primary page dead as of 2026-08-31
suggested_refs: parkour.com, 'The Definitive Origin of Parkour: David Belle's Legacy', a partisan retrospective
sources: parkour.com, 'The Definitive Origin of Parkour: David Belle's Legacy'

stops.name: Paris, the demonstration and Stade 2
stops.date_confidence: attested year, unlocated site. French Wikipedia gives the fire-brigade demonstration, the ninja costume, the Yamakasi name and the Stade 2 broadcast, and credits the broadcast to the Stade 2 team of Francis Maroto, Pierre Sled and Pierre Salviac. The claim that Jean-Francois organised the demonstration and the filming is not supported by either Wikipedia and is not asserted here. No caserne or ceremony site is identified, so the canonical Paris pin is used. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: His half-brother Jean-Francois is a Paris fireman and there is an annual brigade demonstration. Belle brings the Lisses group up to Paris and they perform in ninja costume under the name Yamakasi: a handstand on top of a tower, a backflip off a fire ladder, a discipline with no public existence performed in front of the institution it came out of. France 2's Stade 2 films it and broadcasts the first serious television report on the group. The French word traceur, for the one who runs the line, enters the language out of that coverage.
suggested_refs: The Stade 2 report on Yamakasi, France 2, 1997, produced by Francis Maroto with Pierre Sled and Pierre Salviac

stops.name: Lisses, the hard k
stops.date_confidence: attested etymology, traditional attribution. English Wikipedia states that parkour derives from parcours du combattant and that the actor Hubert Kounde is credited by tradition with proposing the harder k. No document of that conversation exists in any source reached, and the year is not fixed anywhere; 1998 orders the segment.
stops.campa: The thing needs a name. It comes out of parcours, the army's parcours du combattant, and tradition credits the actor Hubert Kounde with proposing that the c be swapped for a k, a harder letter, less like a footpath and more like a blow. Parkour. Belle keeps the word when the circle divides, and the others take theirs. It is his father's private training regime, les parcours, with one consonant changed and a generation added, and the changed letter is the whole distance between a fireman's night habit and something strangers in other countries can join.
suggested_refs: The etymology of parkour from parcours du combattant, with the Kounde attribution recorded as tradition

stops.name: Evry, the circle divides
stops.date_confidence: attested split, undated month. English Wikipedia dates the separation of Belle and Foucan from the group to 1997-1998 and records that the remaining seven kept the name Yamakasi and Foucan's term art du deplacement. Month and day are placeholders. The word freerunning is dated by the same article to Mike Christie's 2003 documentary Jump London, not to the split; Jump London is Foucan's episode, cited here rather than staged as a scene.
stops.campa: Belle and Foucan separate from the group. Seven remain, keeping the name Yamakasi and the term art du deplacement, which Foucan had coined; Belle keeps parkour. The reasons given differ according to who is telling it, and money and television are in every version. Foucan will pick up a third word five years later, freerunning, out of a London documentary made about him, and go his own way with it. One practice, three names, and men who will not entirely speak to one another. English Wikipedia dates the separation to 1997 or 1998 and does not say which.
suggested_refs: Mike Christie's Jump London (2003), where the word freerunning first appears, starring Sebastien Foucan

stops.name: Paris, the film he is not in
stops.date_confidence: attested. Yamakasi: Les Samourais des temps modernes released in France on 4 April 2001, written and produced by Luc Besson but directed by Ariel Zeitoun and Julien Seri; the dossier's description of it as Besson's film is corrected here. Confirmed cast includes Williams Belle, Chau Belle Dinh and Charles Perriere. Belle's absence from the cast is confirmed by convergent filmographies. The Paris pin is the canonical placeholder for the French release, not a location Belle attended.
stops.campa: Yamakasi: Les Samourais des temps modernes opens in France on the fourth of April, written and produced by Luc Besson, directed by Ariel Zeitoun and Julien Seri, starring seven of the men Belle trained with in the Essonne. Williams Belle is in it. Chau Belle Dinh is in it. Charles Perriere is in it. David Belle is not in it. The discipline reaches a French cinema audience for the first time under a name he has stopped using, performed by the half of the circle that kept it.
suggested_refs: Yamakasi: Les Samourais des temps modernes (2001), dir. Ariel Zeitoun and Julien Seri

stops.name: Lisses, a line in the commercial register
stops.date_confidence: attested document, uncertain identification. societe.com, refetched directly, records MONSIEUR DAVID BELLE, SIREN 443 908 991, 17 Allee du Beguinage, 91090 Lisses, APE 741G, created 1 January 2002 and struck off 30 June 2005. The register does not prove the registrant is the traceur rather than a namesake, though the town is his. Coordinates corrected to 48.6129 / 2.4195 per OSM, replacing the dossier's 48.5852 / 2.3978, which is about 3.4 km off; the corrected address sits roughly 250 m from the Dame du Lac.
stops.campa: On the first of January a sole trader is registered at 17 Allee du Beguinage in Lisses under the name Monsieur David Belle, SIREN 443 908 991, classified for business and management consulting. It is struck off on the thirtieth of June 2005. The address stands about two hundred and fifty metres from the Dame du Lac. The entry opens in the year the film work starts and closes three years later, and it is the driest document in the whole record of his life. It does not say whether the registrant is the traceur or a namesake in the same town.
suggested_refs: societe.com record for MONSIEUR DAVID BELLE, SIREN 443 908 991, Lisses

stops.name: London, the rooftops of Rush Hour
stops.date_confidence: reported, primary not fetched. The BBC One ident 'Rush Hour', directed by Tom Carty, with Belle crossing London rooftops and the stunts performed without wires, is reported convergently in secondary accounts of his commercial breakthrough; no BBC primary page was retrieved in this research. Month and day are placeholders inside 2002. The London coordinate is a central-city marker; no rooftop or street is identified in any source consulted. The quote is attributed to Belle through Wikiquote citing BBC News, and bbc.co.uk was unreachable this session.
stops.campa: BBC One commissions an ident from the director Tom Carty in which a man runs home over the rooftops of London to catch the start of a programme. Belle is the man. The BBC makes a point of the stunts being real: no wires, crash mats hidden where a mat can be hidden. Sixty seconds of television put the discipline in front of a national audience that has no word for what it is watching, in a country where the practice does not yet exist and will exist within two years. Which rooftops were used is not stated in any source reached.
stops.quote: Our aim is to take our art to the world and make people understand what it is to move.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to David Belle, cited to BBC News via Wikiquote; the underlying article could not be fetched
suggested_refs: BBC One ident 'Rush Hour' (2002), dir. Tom Carty
sources: parkour.com, 'The Definitive Origin of Parkour: David Belle's Legacy'

stops.name: Paris, a French policeman in Femme Fatale
stops.date_confidence: attested credit, approximate date. English Wikipedia confirms Femme Fatale was shot in Paris; AlloCine independently confirms Belle's credited role as 'le flic francais'. No source reached gives the shooting dates for his scene, so the stop is dated to the release year with placeholder month and day. The canonical Paris pin is used; no shooting location is identified.
stops.campa: Brian De Palma shoots Femme Fatale in Paris and Belle appears in it briefly as a French policeman, credited on AlloCine as le flic francais. The alternative work, for a man with his skill and no diploma, is demonstrations, music videos and advertising, and he has been doing all three since the Stade 2 broadcast. So he takes the part, which does not use the one thing he can do better than anybody alive: a few seconds in uniform, on a Paris street, in somebody else's picture.
suggested_refs: AlloCine filmography for David Belle, fiche personne 93828

stops.name: Paris, Leito in Banlieue 13
stops.date_confidence: attested. Banlieue 13, directed by Pierre Morel, produced and co-written by Luc Besson with Bibi Naceri, released in France 10 November 2004, with Belle as Leito. The Besson quote is reproduced on davidbelleparkour.com's About page with no original interview, publication or date given, and is therefore cited here as an unsourced site attribution. The Paris pin is the film's setting and the canonical placeholder, not an identified shooting location.
stops.campa: Pierre Morel directs, Luc Besson produces and co-writes with Bibi Naceri, and David Belle plays Leito, a man from a walled-off Paris housing estate in a near-future 2010. The film opens with a chase through an apartment block and out across the roofs, performed without wires and without computer assistance, and that one sequence does more for parkour than every demonstration of the preceding decade. The kind of suburb he actually grew up in is now the setting of a French action film, and he is playing the version of himself who still lives there.
stops.quote: Watching him flirt with gravity is something totally amazing. He plays with void, strokes concrete, flies on wind. He can come up with as many stories in mid-air as a ballet dancer on an opera floor.
stops.quote_source: Luc Besson, quoted without source on davidbelleparkour.com, About page
suggested_refs: Banlieue 13 (District B13), 2004, dir. Pierre Morel; the opening chase sequence

stops.name: Barrandov, the Prague soundstages
stops.date_confidence: attested month, corrected coordinates. English Wikipedia's Babylon A.D. article gives February 2007 filming at Barrandov and confirms Belle as 'Hacker Kid', the leader of Darquandier's henchmen who follow Toorop and Aurora to America. The dossier's description of the role as an internet or parkour gang leader is wrong and is not used. Coordinates corrected to 50.0307 / 14.3916, replacing 50.0392 / 14.3922, about 950 m off. Day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He films at Barrandov Studios in Prague in February for Mathieu Kassovitz's Babylon A.D., cast as Hacker Kid, who leads Darquandier's henchmen after Toorop and the girl across a ruined near future. He choreographs movement for an ensemble of roughly ten performers as well as playing the part. The work has become double: the body that does the thing, and the man who teaches ten other bodies a version of it that will read on camera. Nothing here is the Essonne. The obstacles are built by a construction department and struck the same week.
suggested_refs: Babylon A.D. (2008), dir. Mathieu Kassovitz; Barrandov Studios, Prague

stops.name: Ostrava-Poruba, the snow that did not come
stops.date_confidence: attested month, corrected coordinates. English Wikipedia's Babylon A.D. article records March 2007 filming at Ostrava-Poruba after a two-week hiatus caused by inadequate snow. Coordinates corrected to 49.8289 / 18.1669 per English Wikipedia, replacing 49.8346 / 18.1451, about 1.7 km off. Day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The production loses two weeks to weather, there being not enough snow where snow was supposed to be, and moves in March to Ostrava-Poruba in the Czech industrial east to finish. Whatever else the eight hours it once took to cross Lisses to Evry were, they were his own eight hours and nobody was paying for them. This is not that. Belle is a long way from the Essonne, on a schedule, in a coat, waiting, and the waiting is the part nobody films. He is thirty-three, near the top of what a body does, and he spends the weeks between setups sitting down.
suggested_refs: Babylon A.D. second-unit filming, Ostrava-Poruba, March 2007

stops.name: Lisses, the interview at his mother's house
stops.date_confidence: reported, primary inaccessible. Alec Wilkinson's profile 'No Obstacles' in The New Yorker, dated April 2007, is referenced consistently in secondary material; newyorker.com blocked retrieval in this research, so neither the exact date nor the contents were confirmed at first hand. The details of the setting, Monique Kitten's house, Dorine Sane present, Jean-Francois on the money, rest on secondary summary only. Day is a placeholder. The quote is a longer ezboard-cited passage carried by Wikiquote; the platform is defunct and the original post is untraceable.
stops.campa: Alec Wilkinson comes to Lisses for The New Yorker and finds Belle at his mother's house, with his partner Dorine Sane there, a couple of years after Banlieue 13. Jean-Francois tells the writer that people assume the films made his brother rich, and that they did not. The profile becomes one of the fullest accounts of the family in existence, and it is also the moment the traveling begins in earnest: photographers, festivals, people who want a drop rather than a crossing.

Belle is reported afterward to have left the commission, though no reachable source records when. The word he kept in 1998, when the others kept theirs, is now the thing being fought over.

stops.name: Lisses, the wall that gets repainted
stops.date_confidence: attested absence, dated to the present. stops.campa: There is no museum, no statue, no plaque. What exists at Lisses is a wall that traceurs repaint themselves, sanding out the scuff marks their own shoes leave in the render, keeping up a site that belongs to nobody and never had a building. His father's private habit is now a word in four languages, fought over by a gymnastics federation and by the practitioners who refuse its jurisdiction. Belle is fifty-three and still lives in the town. The render will wear through again, and somebody will sand it back again.
